Question B-007-004-002.

Why the correct answer is right: Daytime D-region ionization absorbs low-frequency sky-wave energy. Distant 160-metre and amplitude modulation (AM) broadcast signals often return after the lower region weakens at night.

Why the distractors are wrong:
- sourceIndex 1: "The presence of ionized clouds in the E region": E-region ionization is the wrong layer, and "clouds" is not the D-region absorption mechanism.
- sourceIndex 2: "The splitting of the F region into two sub-regions": The F-region split affects higher ionospheric refraction. It does not explain daylight loss of low-frequency distant stations.
- sourceIndex 3: "The weather below the ionosphere": Lower-atmosphere weather can affect very-high-frequency (VHF) paths and ultra-high-frequency (UHF) paths. It is not why low-frequency sky-wave signals vanish in daytime.
